---
title: "Cross-entropy and KL divergence"
subtitle: "Deriving the objective from target distributions to logits"
lang: en
---

::: {.chapter-lead}
Cross-entropy compares a target distribution $q$ with a predicted distribution $p$. It measures the average cost of using $p$ to encode events distributed according to $q$. Understanding that cost requires connecting it to [Shannon entropy](entropy.qmd) and KL divergence without conflating them.
:::

## Definition

$$
H(q,p)=-\sum_{i=1}^{V}q_i\log p_i.
$$

Here, $q_i\geq0$, $\sum_iq_i=1$, and $p$ is a normalized distribution. Unless stated otherwise, $\log$ denotes the natural logarithm, so values are in nats; using $\log_2$ gives bits. For a one-hot target class $y$, $q_y=1$ and all other entries are zero:

$$
H(q,p)=-\log p_y.
$$

In next-token prediction, $y$ is the observed target token ID at that position. The loss increases when the model assigns a low probability to that token.

## Derivative with respect to logits

With $p_i=\operatorname{softmax}(z)_i$, the one-hot loss is:

$$
\ell(z,y)=-z_y+\log\sum_{j=1}^{V}e^{z_j}.
$$

Differentiating gives:

$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_i}
= -\mathbb{1}[i=y]+\frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}
= p_i-\mathbb{1}[i=y].
$$

The gradient pushes the target logit upward relative to the others and reduces alternative logits according to their probabilities. This formula is for one unweighted position; class weights, label smoothing, and batch reduction change the formula or its scale.

## Cross-entropy, entropy, and KL divergence

Target entropy is $H(q)=-\sum_iq_i\log q_i$. Kullback–Leibler divergence satisfies:

$$
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)=\sum_iq_i\log\frac{q_i}{p_i}
=H(q,p)-H(q).
$$

For a fixed target, minimizing cross-entropy with respect to $p$ therefore also minimizes $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)$. For a one-hot target, $H(q)=0$, so the two quantities are equal.

::: {.callout-warning title="Misconceptions"}
- **“Cross-entropy is a symmetric distance between distributions.”** No: it is not symmetric and is not a distance in the usual sense.
- **“Cross-entropy must lie between 0 and 1.”** No: it can grow arbitrarily large if $p_y$ approaches zero.
- **“CrossEntropyLoss expects probabilities.”** In the usual PyTorch class-index API, it expects unnormalized logits and applies an operation equivalent to log-softmax followed by NLL.
:::

## Interpretation through coding

If events actually follow distribution $q$, but a code is built from probabilities $p$, the ideal length assigned to outcome $i$ is $-\ln p_i$ nats. Its expected length under $q$ is therefore cross-entropy:

$
H(q,p)=-\sum_i q_i\ln p_i.
$

With base-2 logarithms, the same expression is measured in bits. The logarithm base sets the unit but does not change the qualitative conclusions. If $p_i=0$ for an outcome with $q_i>0$, the cost is infinite: the model rules out an event that can occur.

## Why the KL direction matters

The definition of $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)$ and its relationship to $H(q,p)$ are given above. The direction is not decorative: in general, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)\neq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)$ because the expectation is taken under the first distribution. Reversing the arguments therefore changes the penalty.

For example, if $q=(1,0)$ and $p=(0.9,0.1)$, then $H(q,p)=-\log(0.9)$ and $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)=-\log(0.9)$ because $H(q)=0$. The reverse divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)$ is infinite: $p$ assigns positive mass to the second category while $q$ assigns it zero probability. More generally, $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)=+\infty$ whenever $q$ assigns positive mass to an outcome that $p$ assigns zero probability.

## One-hot targets and general target distributions

For a one-hot target of class $y$, the sum reduces to $H(q,p)=-\log p_y$. This is the usual next-token prediction case where one observed token is the target. For a soft target (for example, label smoothing or a teacher distribution), several terms $-q_i\log p_i$ contribute; the loss is no longer just the negative log-probability of one class.

Empirical cross-entropy computed on a corpus is an average over observed targets. It equals the source's true entropy only under ideal conditions, notably when the predictive distribution matches the true conditional distribution. Lower training cross-entropy does not guarantee better generalization: evaluate on separate validation/test data.

## Connection to perplexity

For average cross-entropy in nats $\bar{H}$, perplexity is $\exp(\bar{H})$. If the average is in bits, use $2^{\bar{H}}$. Comparisons require the log base, included token positions, tokenizer, and reduction (sum or mean) to be specified. Perplexity is not a direct measure of factual truth or overall assistant quality.

## Numerical example

If the target is class 2 and $p_2=0.8$, then $\ell=-\log(0.8)\approx0.223$. If $p_2=0.01$, the loss is about $4.605$. A wrong but highly confident prediction is strongly penalized.
